questions.stem: What are the characteristic laboratory findings in primary hypothyroidism?
questions.solutionHtml:
ta" data-dictid="8d4d1904791692777189941782330d">hypothyroidism are elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels and low free thyroxine (T4) levels.
  • This is because, in primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland fails to produce sufficient thyroid hormones, leading to decreased feedback inhibition of the pituitary gland, which in turn increases TSH production to try to stimulate the thyroid gland.

    • Primary vs Secondary Hypothyroidism:

    Feature

    Primary Hypothyroidism

    Secondary Hypothyroidism

    Definition

    Thyroid gland dysfunction leads to inadequate thyroid hormone production

    Pituitary dysfunction leads to insufficient TSH secretion

    Causes
    • Autoimmune (Hashimoto's thyroiditis)
    • Iatrogenic (e.g., post-thyroidectomy, radiation)
    • Iodine deficiency
    • Medications (e.g., amiodarone, lithium)
    • Infiltrative diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis)
    • Food goitrogen → Cabbage, cassava.
    • Pituitary tumors
    • Pituitary surgery or radiation
    • Sheehan’s syndrome
    • Trauma
    • Genetic pituitary hormone deficiencies
    • Non-obstetric cause of pituitary damage called Simmonds's disease (AVM, tumor, HTN)
    • Sarcoidosis
    • Hemochromatosis

    Lab

    TSH - ↑;

    Free T3/T4 - ↓

    TSH - Normal or ↓;

    Free T3/T4 - ↓ (Option D)

    Clinical Features
    • Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance
    • Dry skin, hair loss
    • Bradycardia, constipation
    • Myxedema (puffy face, non-pitting edema)
    • Similar to primary hypothyroidism
    • Other pituitary hormone deficiencies (e.g., low cortisol, low LH/FSH)

    Treatment

    Levothyroxine (T4) replacement with dosage based on TSH levels

    Levothyroxine (T4) replacement, but monitored by free T4 levels (since TSH is unreliable)

    Elevated TSH, low T3 levels (Option B): While low T3 levels can occur in primary hypothyroidism, T4 levels are more commonly measured and are more indicative of thyroid function. Low T3 alone is not specific enough to diagnose primary hypothyroidism without considering T4 levels​

    Elevated TSH, elevated T4 levels (Option C): This combination is not characteristic of primary hypothyroidism. Elevated TSH with elevated T4 levels might indicate resistance to thyroid hormone or a rare TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, but not primary hypothyroidism​



    Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, Volume I, Page. 2933

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones use receptor tyrosine kinase signalling?
questions.solutionHtml:
(RTKs)
  • Enzyme-linked receptors located on cell membranes.
  • Pass through the membrane once; the hormone-binding site is extracellular, and the catalytic site is intracellular.

Mechanism of Action:

  • Hormone Binding: Hormone binds to the extracellular part of the RTK.
  • Enzyme Activation: Binding activates or inactivates an intracellular enzyme. Some RTKs have intrinsic enzymatic activity, while others depend on associated enzymes.

Example: Leptin Receptor

  • Family: Cytokine receptors.
  • Hormone: Leptin (regulates appetite and energy balance).
  • Associated Enzyme: JAK2 (Janus kinase family).

Signaling Process:

  • Dimerization: Leptin binding causes receptor dimerization.
  • Phosphorylation & Conformation Change: Leptin binding alters receptor conformation, phosphorylating the intracellular part of the JAK receptor.

Intracellular Signaling:

  • Activated JAK2 phosphorylates tyrosine residues within the receptor-JAK2 complex, activating STAT proteins, which leads to target gene activation and protein synthesis.
  • JAK2 also activates additional pathways, including MAPK and PI3K.

Effects:

  • Rapid: Due to activation of the above-said intracellular enzymes.
  • Slower: Requires new protein synthesis.

Hormones Utilising Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Signalling:

  • Fibroblast Growth Factor
  • Growth Hormone
  • Hepatocyte Growth Factor
  • Insulin (Option A)
  • Insulin-like Growth Factor-1
  • Leptin
  • Prolactin
  • Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor

TSH (Option B), TRH (Option C), and MSH (Option D):

  • Belong to the family of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and signal through G-protein-mediated pathways.
  • TSH acts on the thyroid gland to stimulate the production and release of thyroid hormones, while TRH regulates TSH release from the pituitary gland.
  • It is a peptide hormone that regulates pigmentation and is primarily involved in the activation of melanocortin receptors, which are also GPCRs.


Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14th Edition, Page 920-925

questions.stem: Among the given options, which condition is expected to exhibit the greatest levels of ACTH and cortisol?
questions.solutionHtml:
is a condition characterized by the overproduction of ACTH by a pituitary tumor (adenoma).
  • This excessive ACTH production leads to increased stimulation of the adrenal glands, causing them to produce and release excessive amounts of cortisol, a stress hormone.
  • Therefore, both ACTH and cortisol levels are elevated in Cushing's disease.

    •  

    Corticosteroid feedback mechanism

     

    • Circadian rhythm: Diurnal pattern with peak in morning and low in evening, independent of external factors (Option A ruled out)
    • The adrenal cortex atrophies and becomes unresponsive to the ACTH for about six months after a prolonged treatment with steroids. (Option B ruled out)
    • Adrenal insufficiency is precipitated as a result.

     

    Addison's disease (Option C): It is characterized by a deficiency of cortisol production due to adrenal insufficiency. In this condition, both ACTH and cortisol levels are decreased. ACTH levels are elevated as a compensatory mechanism to stimulate the adrenal glands, but the adrenal glands are unable to produce sufficient cortisol.




    Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition, page 344-346, 348-350, 342, 343
    OP GHAI Essentials of Pediatrics,10th edition, Page 543-547

questions.stem: Which among the following hormones, in a lactating mother, is responsible for the growth of breast tissue?
questions.solutionHtml:
eta" data-dictid="760a997a7b1692777196db9355b82a">prolactin is primarily responsible for stimulating the growth and development of the milk-producing breast tissue (lobuloalveolar structures).

Prolactin

Source

Secreted by lactotrophs of the anterior pituitary (number increase during pregnancy, lactation, estrogen therapy)

Synthesis
  • Synthesized as preprolactin → proprolactin → prolactin
  • Stored in granules of lactotrophs → secreted upon stimulation

Factors Controlling Secretion

Increased by:

  • Prolactin Releasing Factor (PRF)
  • Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH) (B)
  • Pregnancy, estrogen therapy, breastfeeding
  • Sleep, stress (D)
  • Oxytocin, serotonin, Angiotensin-II (A)
  • Dopamine antagonists, opioids

Decreased by:

  • Dopamine and its agonists
  • Somatostatin, GABA
  • Prolactin (feedback mechanism)

Functions
  • Milk Synthesis and Secretion: Stimulates milk synthesis and secretion
  • Breast Development:
    • Hyperplasia of breast tissue (puberty, pregnancy and lactation)
    • Stimulates development of mammary glands
    • Works with estrogen, progesterone, cortisol, GH, insulin
  • Reproductive Functions:
    • Inhibits GnRH (prevents ovulation,cause lactational amenorrhea)
    • Inhibition of libido, stimulation of maternal behaviour
    • Decreases spermatogenesis in males
  • Immunity: Synthesized by immunocytes (balance immune response during pregnancy).
  • Liver: Increases synthesis of synlactin (intermediary growth factor).

Clinical Correlation
  • Amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome due to hyperprolactinemia
  • Diagnosis: High plasma prolactin levels, pituitary MRI
  • Treatment: Dopaminergic drugs to inhibit prolactin secretion, restoring fertility and libido

Incorrect Options:

Oxytocin (Option A) triggers milk ejection (let-down reflex), not growth.

Estrogen (Option B) stimulates ductal growth in the breast tissue and also promotes overall breast enlargement and structural development.

Progesterone (Option D) supports lobuloalveolar development, preparing the breast for milk production.
